intro: Four modules take you from your first script to useful automation: Python basics and virtual environments, decisions, loops and data structures, reading files and parsing logs, and running programs, handling errors and calling APIs safely. Practice in the labs and keep the Reference tab handy.

modules.title: Python basics and running scripts
modules.summary: Install and run Python, work with values, strings and user input, and keep projects tidy with virtual environments.

blocks.p: Python is readable, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and has a huge standard library. IT staff use it to process logs and spreadsheets, call APIs, automate repetitive tasks and glue tools together. You save a script in a .py file and run it with python script.py (on some systems python3).

blocks.note: Check your version with python --version. Use a current supported Python 3 release.

blocks.p: Variables just name a value: host = "server01". Format text with f-strings: f"Checking {host}". Read input with input() (it always returns text) and convert with int() when you need a number.

guide.h: Run scripts and keep dependencies separate

steps.d: pip install requests, then record with pip freeze > requirements.txt.

tips: Python uses indentation (usually 4 spaces) to define blocks. Be consistent.
Use a virtual environment per project so package versions do not clash.
Read error messages from the bottom up: the last line says what went wrong.
terms: A text file of Python code that you run.
A name that refers to a value.
An isolated folder of packages for one project (venv).

slides.title: Python for IT work
script: Python is a friendly language that IT teams use to automate repetitive work.

slides.title: Values and strings
script: Python values have types. Use f-strings to build messages.

slides.title: Running a script
script: Save your code in a file and run it with Python. If it fails, read the error message from the bottom up.

slides.title: Virtual environments
script: A virtual environment keeps each project's packages separate.

visual.text:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt

modules.title: Decisions, loops, lists, dictionaries and functions
modules.summary: Control the flow of a script and organize data with lists and dictionaries, then reuse code with functions.

blocks.p: if, elif and else choose a path. for repeats over items; while repeats until a condition is false.

blocks.p: Add with hosts.append("web3"). Loop over a dictionary with for key, value in server.items():. Comprehensions such as [h.upper() for h in hosts] build lists in one line.
A function packages steps you reuse. Define it with def, give it parameters and return a result.

blocks.note: Keep functions small and named for what they do: is_port_open(), parse_line().

tips: A single = assigns; == compares. Mixing them up is a classic bug.
Do not change a list while looping over it; build a new list instead.
Use dictionaries when you look things up by name, lists when order matters.

slides.title: Making decisions
script: Use if statements to choose what your script does.

slides.title: Loops
script: A for loop repeats code for each item in a list.

slides.title: Lists and dictionaries
script: Lists hold ordered items. Dictionaries look up values by key.

slides.title: Functions
script: Wrap repeated logic in a function so you can reuse and test it.

modules.title: Files, text processing and structured data
modules.summary: Read and write files, parse log lines and work with CSV and JSON.

blocks.p: Open files with a with block so they close automatically.

blocks.note: Mode "w" erases the existing file. Use "a" to append.

blocks.p: Strings have helpful methods: line.strip(), line.split(), "ERROR" in line, line.startswith(...), .replace(). For patterns, the re module handles regular expressions.

blocks.p: The standard library reads both. CSV is rows and columns; JSON is nested data from APIs and config files.

tips: Always handle files with with; never leave them open.
Test on a small copy of the data first.

Comma-separated values, one record per line.

slides.title: Read a log
script: A with block opens a file and closes it for you. Loop over the lines to process a log.

slides.title: Count things
bullets: Sort to find the top items
script: A dictionary makes a handy counter, for example hits per IP address.

slides.title: CSV and JSON
script: CSV and JSON are the common formats you will read and produce.

slides.title: Careful with writes
script: Opening a file in write mode replaces it. Use append, or write a new file, when you are not sure.

modules.title: Automating IT tasks safely
modules.summary: Run programs, work with the file system, handle errors, accept arguments and call web APIs responsibly.

guide.h: Run commands and work with files

blocks.p: subprocess.run launches other programs and captures their output. shutil copies and moves files, and os / pathlib handle paths.

cmds: Run a program (pass arguments as a list)
head: Code
Meaning

blocks.note: Avoid building shell commands from user input with shell=True: it invites command injection. Pass an argument list instead.

blocks.p: Wrap risky steps in try / except and catch specific errors, such as FileNotFoundError. Use argparse to let people pass options when they run your script: python check.py --host web1. Use the logging module instead of lots of print calls.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Levels such as INFO and ERROR, optionally to a file
Return a non-zero exit code on failure

blocks.p: The requests package (install with pip) calls web APIs: requests.get(url, timeout=10). Always set a timeout and check response.raise_for_status().

list: Keep tokens and passwords out of the script: read them from environment variables (os.environ["API_TOKEN"]) or a secrets manager
Run scripts on a schedule with cron (Linux/macOS) or Task Scheduler (Windows)
Test with a dry-run option before a script changes or deletes anything

tips: Add a --dry-run option to any script that changes things.
Log what the script does so you can audit it later.
Never hard-code secrets, and never commit them to Git.
terms: An error raised while code runs; handled with try/except.
A number returned to the OS; 0 means success.
An interface for programs to talk to a service, often over HTTP.
A setting provided by the OS, used for secrets and configuration.

slides.title: Run other programs
script: Python can run any command-line tool and read its output.

visual.text:
import subprocess
r = subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", "web1"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.returncode)

slides.title: Handle errors
script: Handle expected errors so a script fails clearly instead of crashing.

slides.title: Call an API
script: Use requests to call a web API. Always set a timeout and read secrets from the environment.

visual.text:
import os, requests
r = requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": os.environ["API_TOKEN"]}, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
print(r.json())

slides.title: Automate responsibly
bullets: Schedule with cron or Task Scheduler
script: Test with a dry run, log what you do and only then schedule the script.
